papers.title_in_file: Financial Risk Management on a Neutral Atom Quantum Processor
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sections I-III (dataset, QBoost, QUBO, results, limitations), Conclusions; appendices not read
papers.what_it_is: A PASQAL and Credit Agricole CIB study of a QBoost-inspired quantum-enhanced classifier for credit-rating downgrade (fallen angel) prediction, run on a neutral atom QPU up to 60 qubits and on tensor-network simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classifier trained on the QPU reached 27.9% precision against 28% for the Random Forest benchmark at a recall of approximately 83%, using 50 learners against 1200 for the Random Forest.
quotes: We report that the proposed classifier trained on QPU achieved competitive performance with 27.9% precision against the benchmarked 28% precision for the same recall of approximately 83%.
However, the proposed approach outperformed its classical counterpart with respect to interpretability with only 50 learners employed versus 1200 for the Random Forest and comparable runtimes.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single empirical study on one dataset; the authors' own run.
assertions.reader_inference: The QPU-trained model matched but did not beat the classical benchmark on precision.

assertions.value: The authors state the dataset holds more than 90 000 instances with around 150 features from public data over 20 years.
quotes: The dataset used in this study originates from public data over a period of 20 years (2001-2020).
It comprises of more than 90 000 instances characterized by around 150 features, representing the historical evolution of credit ratings as well as numerous financial variables.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its dataset, Section I.A.

assertions.value: The authors report that the boosting variant reached 29% precision, but it was trained with a quantum-inspired tensor-network optimizer because it cannot be trained on current hardware.
assertions.anchor: Conclusions and Outlook, p.12; Section III.C
quotes: achieving a precision of 29%, 1% above the benchmark, with just 90 learners (against 1200)
although is not amenable to be trained on current hardware, was trained using a quantum-inspired optimizer based on Tensor Networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the limit on hardware is the authors' own statement.
assertions.reader_inference: The only result above the benchmark was obtained without a QPU.

assertions.value: The authors state that, extrapolating from their results, the quantum classifiers could outperform the benchmark within a few hundred addressable qubits.
quotes: Extrapolating from these results and keeping other factors constant, the proposed quantum classifiers could outperform the benchmarked model within a few hundred addressable qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Projection from linear extrapolation of a handful of points; not run.

papers.title_in_file: Implementing Slack-Free Custom Penalty Function for QUBO on Gate-Based Quantum Computers
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section V Results, Section VI Discussion, Section VII Conclusion; derivations in Sections III-IV skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A VQE-based treatment of inequality constraints in the Multiple Knapsack Problem using exponential and step penalty functions in place of slack variables.

assertions.value: The authors report that the step penalty achieved higher feasibility and optimality rates than the slack-based and unbalanced quadratic penalties, with a mean optimality gap close to the unbalanced penalty.
quotes: On the other hand, the step penalty function achieved higher feasibility and optimality rate compared to the slack-based penalty and the unbalanced quadratic penalty, while having a mean optimality gap that is close to that of the unbalanced penalty.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated experiment on small instances.

assertions.value: The authors report that the exponential penalty reached a highest feasibility rate of 99%, while the unbalanced quadratic penalty kept the highest optimality rate, 40%.
quotes: The feasibility rate achieves the highest of 99% for the exponential function, whereas the quadratic penalty (unbalanced) still has the highest optimality rate of 40%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated experiment; Table II.

assertions.value: The authors state they solved 78 instances of the Multiple Knapsack Problem, needing 9 to 12 qubits, with Qiskit statevector simulation.
quotes: We solve 78 instances of MKP with at most 3 knapsacks and 4 items.
we require 9 to 12 qubits to encode the problem as quantum states.
The ansatz circuit is simulated using Qiskit statevector simulation [18].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup and scope.
assertions.reader_inference: All results come from noiseless simulation of at most 12 qubits.

assertions.value: The authors state that the step penalty's computational cost scales exponentially with the number of terms in a single constraint.
quotes: its computational cost scales exponentially with the number of terms in a single constraint (Theorem 1).
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' stated limit, Section VI.

papers.title_in_file: How many qubits does a machine learning problem require?
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 3 theorem statements, Section 4 summary and results text, Section 6 Discussion; proofs and the training demonstration not read in detail
papers.what_it_is: A Coherent Computing paper showing that bit-bit encoding gives universal approximation for classification and defining a qubit-count resource metric Qdataset(x).

assertions.value: The authors state they prove that bit-bit encoding inherently ensures universal approximation.
quotes: We proved that bit-bit encoding inherently ensures universal approximation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems 1 and 2, Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors report that medium-sized classical benchmark classification datasets need a Qdataset(1.0) of 27 qubits on average.
quotes: We find that medium-sized classical benchmark classification datasets have a Qdataset(1.0) of 27 on average.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result over a set of benchmark datasets.

assertions.value: The authors state they cannot theoretically prove that their encoding is optimal.
quotes: While we cannot theoretically prove that we have an optimal encoding, if the dimensionality reduction scheme produces independent features, it is close to optimal in an information theoretical sense.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit, Section 6.

assertions.value: The authors state with moderate confidence that a dataset needing more than about 50 qubits to encode is a candidate for quantum advantage within this framework, and that several datasets studied so far may not be.
quotes: we can thus state with moderate confidence that if a dataset can requires more than about 50 qubits to encode, it is a candidate for quantum advantage within this framework.
This, in turn, indicates that several datasets that have been studied in the quantum literature so far may not be candidates for quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author inference resting on the classical simulation limit; not proved.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Optimization via Gradient-Based Hamiltonian Descent
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, theorem statements in Sections 4-5, Section 6 numerical results text, Section 7 Conclusion; appendix proofs not read
papers.what_it_is: An ICML 2025 paper that adds gradient information to Quantum Hamiltonian Descent for continuous unconstrained optimization, with convergence proofs and 2D simulations.

assertions.value: The authors state they prove convergence of gradient-based QHD dynamics in function values and gradient norms by a Lyapunov function approach.
quotes: We prove the convergence of the gradient-based QHD dynamics in both function values and gradient norms via a Lyapunov function approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems 1 and 4 (continuous time).

assertions.value: The authors report that on the Cube-Wave function the final objective value of gradient-based QHD is nearly an order of magnitude lower than QHD and two orders of magnitude lower than SGDM and NAG.
quotes: In the Cube-Wave function, for instance, the final objective value obtained by gradient-based QHD is nearly an order of magnitude lower than that of QHD and two orders of magnitude lower than those achieved by SGDM and NAG.
assertions.certainty_reason: Classical simulation on a small number of test functions.

assertions.value: The authors state the numerical experiments are limited to 2D problems because of exponential growth of computational overhead, and the analysis is for continuous time.
quotes: The numerical experiments are limited to 2D problems due to the exponential growth of computational overhead.
Our theoretical analysis has primarily focused on the convergence of gradient-based QHD in continuous time, while the long-term behavior of the discrete-time algorithm deserves further investigation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' stated limits, Section 7.

papers.title_in_file: Hybrid Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Network: Towards Efficient Learning of High-Speed Flows
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sections 3.1-3.3 results text, discussion list, Section 4 Conclusion; appendix tables not read in detail
papers.what_it_is: An A*STAR benchmark of hybrid quantum PINNs against classical PINNs and quantum PINNs on harmonic, discontinuous and transonic flow problems, run by classical emulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that quantum PINNs are highly efficient on harmonic problems but struggle to generalize on non-harmonic settings with shocks and discontinuities, and that hybrid models mitigate such artifacts.
quotes: Quantum PINNs are highly efficient for harmonic problems achieving the lowest loss with minimal parameters due to their Fourier structure, but struggle to generalize in non-harmonic settings involving shocks and discontinuities.
HQPINNs mitigate such artifacts, and with sufficient parameterization, can match the performance of classical models in more complex regimes.
assertions.certainty_reason: Emulated benchmark on three flow problems.

assertions.value: The authors report that the best hybrid model has a reduced parameter count of 484 against 1505.
quotes: The hybrid model hy-10-4-2 achieves strong balanced performance with high accuracy and trainability, as well as reduced parameter count (484 vs. 1505).
assertions.certainty_reason: One benchmark case, Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that simulating the quantum circuits classically gives per-epoch runtimes up to 100 times slower than fully classical models, a constraint on scalability.
quotes: Quantum emulation cost is a constraint.
Simulating PQCs classically results in per-epoch runtimes up to 100
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured runtime from the authors' emulation.

assertions.value: The authors state the hybrid model is currently limited by the relatively small quantum sub-network, which cannot cope with the shock features of the aerofoil problem.
quotes: the HQPINN is currently limited by the relatively small scale of quantum sub-network which is unable to cope with more complex shock features of the aerofoil problem, which degrades the overall performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' stated limit, Section 4.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum advantage for learning shallow neural networks with natural data distributions
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section II results and informal theorems, Section III Discussion, Section IV Methods overview; appendix proofs not read
papers.what_it_is: A Google Quantum AI learning-theory paper giving an efficient quantum SQ algorithm for learning periodic neurons over non-uniform distributions and classical hardness for gradient-based and correlational SQ algorithms.

assertions.value: The authors state they design an efficient QSQ quantum algorithm for learning periodic neurons over non-uniform distributions and prove the problem hard for classical gradient-based and a more general class of SQ algorithms, establishing an exponential quantum advantage.
quotes: Our work helps close the gap between these two regimes by designing an efficient quantum algorithm for learning periodic neurons in the QSQ model over a variety of non-uniform distributions and the first explicit treatment of real-valued functions.

We prove that this problem is hard not only for classical gradient-based algorithms, which are the workhorses of machine learning, but also for a more general class of SQ algorithms, establishing an exponential quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems proved in the appendices; scope of hardness limited as in the stated limit.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's wording on SQ algorithms is broader than the Discussion's own scope statement.

assertions.value: The authors state the classical hardness holds only against classical gradient methods and correlational SQ algorithms (for Gaussian distributions).
quotes: First, the classical hardness for our results only holds against classical gradient methods and correlational SQ algorithms (for Gaussian distributions).
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' stated limit, Section III.

assertions.value: The authors state the practical origin of the quantum example state is an open question and that coherent loading of classical data can be costly and eliminate an end-to-end quantum advantage.
quotes: One question that has persisted around many quantum learning results, including the present work, is the practical origin of the quantum example state
Instead, one may consider coherently loading the data from known classical examples, but this can be costly and eliminate an end-to-end quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' stated limit, Section III.

papers.title_in_file: A Novel Spatial-Temporal Variational Quantum Circuit to Enable Deep Learning on NISQ Devices
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section VI evaluation text on real devices and nonlinear dataset, Section VII Conclusion; design sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A George Mason University design (ST-VQC) with a nonlinear spatial encoder, SWAP-free circuit and RL-based hyperparameter search, evaluated on IBM devices.

assertions.value: The authors report that on MNIST-2 the existing VQC dropped from over 90% simulated accuracy to approximately 50% on real quantum computers, while ST-VQC reached 90% accuracy on real quantum computers.
quotes: Experimental results on MNIST-2 showed that while the existing VQC achieved over 90% accuracy in simulation, its accuracy dropped to approximately 50% when deployed on real quantum computers, rendering it ineffective.
In contrast, the proposed framework demonstrated the ability to find a quantum learning circuit with an accuracy of 90% on real quantum computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single empirical study on two IBM devices, binary MNIST.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a nonlinear synthetic dataset ST-VQC averaged 94.71% accuracy on the ideal simulator while VQC averaged 49.53%.
quotes: Specifically, on the ideal simulator, ST-VQC can achieve an accuracy of 94.71% on average while VQC can only have an accuracy of 49.53% on average.
assertions.certainty_reason: Synthetic dataset, simulator result.

assertions.value: The authors state ST-VQC was evaluated on two IBM processors, ibm cairo with 27 qubits and ibmq lima with 7 qubits.
quotes: The proposed ST-VQC has been evaluated on two IBM quantum processors, ibm cairo with 27 qubits and ibmq lima with 7 qubits, to assess its effectiveness.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup.

papers.title_in_file: AI-Powered Algorithm-Centric Quantum Processor Topology Design
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 5 Discussion and Conclusion, appendix benchmark note; method and experiment sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Qtailor, a reinforcement-learning method that designs a quantum processor qubit topology for each circuit to reduce mapped circuit depth.

assertions.value: The authors report a minimum of 20% reduction in circuit depth in 60% of the cases examined and a maximum enhancement of up to 46%.
quotes: Experiments demonstrate that we have achieved notable enhancements in circuit performance, with a minimum of 20% reduction in circuit depth in 60% of the cases examined, and a maximum enhancement of up to 46%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single empirical study on benchmark circuits.

assertions.value: The authors state the benefits in reducing circuit depth become increasingly evident as the scale of the quantum circuits increases.
quotes: Furthermore, the pronounced benefits of our approach in reducing circuit depth become increasingly evident as the scale of the quantum circuits increases, exhibiting the scalability of our method in terms of problem size.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical trend over the tested circuit sizes.

assertions.value: The authors state the study focuses on connectivity constraints and that other physical systems or fabrication processes may entail distinct constraints.
quotes: In the current study, we have focused on the connectivity constraints of quantum processors, an essential factor in processor design.
However, different quantum physical systems or varying fabrication processes for quantum processors may entail distinct constraints.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' stated scope and limit, Section 5.
